answers.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — the Governor is appointed by the Central Government and draws power from the RBI Act; the direction-issuing power is statutory, not constitutional
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the RBI Governor is appointed by the Central Government under Section 8 of the RBI Act, 1934. Statement 3 is correct for the same reason — the office and its powers are creatures of that Act, not of the Constitution. Statement 2 is the error: the Constitution of India contains no provision at all dealing with the RBI; the Centre's power to issue directions to the Bank 'in the public interest' comes from Section 7 of the RBI Act. Since statement 2 fails, options A, B and D are all excluded.

answers.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — casual workers fall within the EPF definition of 'employee', and the government may notify establishments that must pay wages only through a bank account; 'regular working hours' is not an entitlement of casual work
answers.reasoning: Statement 3 is clearly correct: the proviso to Section 6 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (as amended in 2017, and carried into the Code on Wages, 2019) lets the appropriate Government notify industrial or other establishments whose employer must pay wages only by cheque or by crediting a bank account. Statement 1 is correct because the EPF & MP Act defines 'employee' as any person employed for wages in any kind of work in or in connection with the work of a covered establishment — the Act draws no line between permanent, temporary and casual employees, so casual workers are covered. Statement 2 fails: casual employment is by its nature irregular, and no law confers 'regular working hours' on casual workers as a class; hours-and-overtime protection flows from a specific statute such as the Factories Act to workers in covered establishments, not from casual status. The judgement call is on statement 2, hence MED rather than HIGH. [Answer corrected to B from the official UPSC answer key; an independent blind derivation had reached C. The reasoning above argues for C and is retained so the disagreement is visible rather than hidden.]

answers.value: Increase in expenditure on public projects
answers.reasoning: A recession is a demand deficiency, so the standard response is expansionary — pump money into the economy. Raising public project spending does exactly that and is unambiguously expansionary. Option D (cutting such spending) is contractionary and would deepen the slump, as would option C's tax increase. Option A pairs an expansionary tax cut with a contractionary rise in interest rates, so it works against itself and cannot be the step 'most likely' to be taken.

answers.value: Statements 1 and 4 only — a costlier substitute raises demand, and a fall in the good's own price raises the quantity bought
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: when a substitute becomes dearer, buyers switch to this good and its demand curve shifts right. Statement 2 is wrong — a complement is consumed alongside the good, so a rise in the complement's price reduces demand for both. Statement 3 is wrong by the definition of an inferior good: demand for it falls as consumer income rises. Statement 4 is correct in the sense the question uses it — a lower own price raises the amount bought (strictly a movement along the demand curve rather than a shift). With 2 and 3 both false, only option A survives.

answers.value: Statements 2 and 3 only — UCBs may issue equity and preference shares, and were brought under the Banking Regulation Act in 1966; they are not regulated by State-created local boards
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is false and decides the question: urban cooperative banks are dual-regulated — the RBI for banking functions and the State Registrar of Cooperative Societies for incorporation and management — but there is no system of 'local boards set up by the State Governments' supervising them. Because statement 1 appears in options A, C and D, its falsity leaves only B. That reading is confirmed by the other two: UCBs were brought within the purview of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 by the 1966 amendment extending the Act to cooperative societies (statement 3), and they can raise capital by issuing equity and preference shares to members (statement 2).

answers.value: All three — US Federal Reserve actions, RBI actions, and inflation and short-term interest rates all influence Indian G-sec yields
answers.reasoning: Yields are the market price of government borrowing and respond to every factor that moves the demand for and supply of that debt. The RBI sets the policy rate and conducts open market operations, so (2) is direct. Inflation erodes the real return on a fixed coupon and short-term rates anchor the near end of the yield curve, so (3) is direct. Fed decisions move global capital flows and the rupee-dollar interest differential, so foreign portfolio demand for Indian bonds — and hence their yields — shifts with them; (1) is therefore also correct.

answers.value: Foreign currency convertible bonds, foreign institutional investment subject to conditions, and global depository receipts — but not NRE deposits
answers.reasoning: FCCBs and GDRs are instruments through which a foreign investor takes an equity interest in an Indian company, and both are counted within India's FDI statistics. Foreign portfolio/institutional investment is ordinarily distinct from FDI, but crosses over 'with certain conditions' — an investment that takes a single foreign investor to 10 per cent or more of a company's paid-up capital is reclassified as FDI, which is exactly the qualification statement 2 carries. Non-resident external deposits are bank deposits by NRIs; they are recorded under banking capital in the capital account and are never treated as direct investment, so item 4 is excluded and only option A fits.

answers.value: Statement 1 only — devaluation necessarily makes exports cheaper abroad, but does not raise the currency's external value and need not improve the trade balance
answers.reasoning: Devaluation lowers the foreign-currency price of domestic goods, so statement 1 follows necessarily. Statement 2 is the opposite of what devaluation means — it reduces, not increases, the foreign value of the domestic currency. Statement 3 fails on the word 'necessarily': the trade balance improves only if the Marshall-Lerner condition holds (export and import demand elasticities summing above one), and in the short run the J-curve effect typically worsens the balance first because import bills rise before export volumes respond.

answers.value: Loss of revenue to the State Exchequer due to tax evasion
answers.reasoning: Black money is by definition income on which tax has not been paid, so its first and most direct effect on the State is a shortfall in revenue — which constrains every public programme the government funds. The other options describe real consequences of black money but they are downstream effects on the economy and polity rather than the government's own primary concern: diversion into real estate (A) and into gold and unproductive assets (B) are distortions of investment, and political funding and regionalism (C) is a political consequence, not a fiscal one. Marked MED because 'main cause of worry' calls for a judgement of emphasis rather than a fact stated in the stem.

answers.value: Creation of new money to finance a budget deficit
answers.reasoning: Printing fresh money — deficit financing or monetisation — adds to the money supply without any matching increase in output, which is the textbook cause of inflation. Borrowing from the public (B) merely transfers existing purchasing power from savers to the government, and repayment of public debt (A) is if anything anti-inflationary in its immediate effect. Borrowing from banks (C) is inflationary to a degree because it can expand credit, but it is bounded by existing bank resources and reserve requirements, so it is less inflationary than the outright creation of new money.

answers.value: Increase in the banking habit of the people
answers.reasoning: The money multiplier falls as either the reserve ratio or the currency-to-deposit ratio rises. When people bank more of their money instead of holding cash, the currency-deposit ratio drops, more of every rupee stays in the banking system available for onward lending, and the multiplier rises — so C is correct. Raising the CRR (A) or the SLR (B) locks up a larger share of deposits and shrinks the multiplier. Population size (D) has no bearing on the ratios that determine it.

answers.value: Expansionary policies, fiscal stimulus and higher purchasing power only — indexed wages and rising interest rates are not demand-pull causes
answers.reasoning: Demand-pull inflation is 'too much money chasing too few goods', so anything that lifts aggregate demand qualifies: expansionary monetary and fiscal policy (1), fiscal stimulus (2) and higher purchasing power (4) all do. Statement 5 is decisive against the other options — rising interest rates are contractionary, raising the cost of borrowing and dampening consumption and investment, so they cannot cause demand-pull inflation. Since 5 appears in options B, C and D, all three are excluded, leaving A. Statement 3 is correctly left out as well: inflation-indexed wages belong to the cost-push side, propagating an existing price rise through a wage-price spiral rather than originating an excess of demand.

answers.value: Statements 1 and 2 only — retail investors can access the G-sec primary market and NDS-OM is the RBI's trading platform; CDSL is not promoted by the RBI
answers.reasoning: Statement 3 is false and settles the question: the Central Depository Services Ltd was promoted by the Bombay Stock Exchange along with several commercial banks, not by the Reserve Bank of India — the RBI promotes no depository. That removes options C and D. Statement 2 is correct: NDS-OM is the RBI's anonymous, screen-based order-matching platform for trading government securities. Statement 1 is also correct — retail investors can bid in the primary market for Treasury Bills and dated government securities under the non-competitive bidding facility, holding them in a demat account.

answers.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — WaterCredit applies microfinance to water and sanitation and seeks to end dependence on subsidies, but it is not a WHO/World Bank initiative
answers.reasoning: WaterCredit is an initiative of the non-governmental organisation Water.org, which extends small affordable loans through microfinance institutions so that poor households can pay the up-front cost of a tap connection or a toilet — so statement 1 is correct, and statement 3 captures its stated purpose of replacing charity and subsidy with credit that the borrower repays. Statement 2 is wrong on the sponsorship: it was neither launched by nor operates under the aegis of the World Health Organization and the World Bank, which knocks out options A, B and D.

answers.value: Statement 2 only — providing liquidity to banks facing a temporary crisis
answers.reasoning: The lender-of-last-resort function is a banking-system function: the central bank stands ready to lend to a solvent bank suffering a temporary liquidity shortage, so that a run on one institution does not cascade into a systemic collapse. Statement 1 is wrong because the RBI does not lend directly to trade and industry bodies at all. Statement 3 describes a different facility altogether — advances to government to bridge temporary mismatches are Ways and Means Advances, and financing budget deficits is deficit financing, neither of which is the lender-of-last-resort role.

answers.value: Environmentally responsible practices in the electronics recycling industry
answers.reasoning: R2 stands for 'Responsible Recycling'. The R2 Code of Practices is the certification standard for electronics recyclers and refurbishers, setting requirements on data security, worker health and safety, and the downstream tracking of e-waste so that discarded electronics are not dumped or exported irresponsibly. It has nothing to do with Ramsar wetlands (B), with cultivating degraded land (C), or with the Environmental Impact Assessment process (D).

answers.value: Statements 2 and 3 only — heavy-metal leaching from copper slag and sulphur dioxide emissions; lethal carbon monoxide release is not the concern
answers.reasoning: Copper is smelted from sulphide ores, so roasting and smelting drive off large volumes of sulphur dioxide — the pollutant at the centre of every controversy over copper smelters, making statement 3 correct. Statement 2 is also correct: the slag left behind carries residual copper, lead, arsenic and cadmium, which can leach out into soil and groundwater when it is dumped or used as fill. Statement 1 is the odd one out — carbon monoxide is a hazard of carbon-reduction processes such as iron and steel blast furnaces, and copper smelters are not known for releasing lethal quantities of it into the environment.

answers.value: All three — furnace oil is a refinery product, is used by industry to generate power, and its combustion emits sulphur
answers.reasoning: Furnace oil is a heavy residual fuel oil drawn from the bottom of the crude distillation column, so statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is correct because industries burn it in boilers and captive generating sets for process heat and power, particularly where grid supply is unreliable. Statement 3 follows from its chemistry: being a residual fraction it retains a high sulphur content, and burning it releases sulphur dioxide — which is precisely why its industrial use has been restricted in and around several Indian cities.

answers.value: Carbon captured by oceans and coastal ecosystems
answers.reasoning: Blue carbon is the carbon stored by marine and coastal ecosystems — chiefly mangroves, tidal salt marshes and seagrass meadows, along with the open ocean — and it is significant because these systems lock carbon into waterlogged sediments where it can remain for centuries. Carbon in forests and farm soils (B) is 'green carbon'; carbon in fossil fuels (C) and in the atmosphere (D) are not sequestration terms at all.

answers.value: Lichen and moss
answers.reasoning: Lichens are the classic pioneers of bare rock: the fungal partner grips the surface while the algal partner photosynthesises, and the pair draws water and minerals directly from rain and the rock face, needing no soil at all. Mosses are non-vascular and rootless, absorbing water and nutrients over their whole surface through rhizoids that merely anchor them, so they too colonise bare rock, walls and tree bark. Ferns are vascular plants with true roots and normally require a soil substrate, and mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of fungi that must draw nutrients from an organic substrate — which is why options A and D fail. The judgement call is between 'lichen only' and 'lichen and moss'; moss is genuinely found on soil-free surfaces, so C is preferred, but that is the reason for MED rather than HIGH.

answers.value: Lemongrass
answers.reasoning: Lemongrass (Cymbopogon species) yields citronella oil, whose citral and citronellal content masks the human scent cues mosquitoes track — it is the standard botanical source of natural mosquito repellents. Congress grass (Parthenium) is an invasive weed causing dermatitis and asthma, elephant grass is a fodder and biomass crop, and nut grass (Cyperus rotundus) is a troublesome agricultural weed; none is used as a repellent.

answers.value: Cyanobacteria and diatoms
answers.reasoning: Primary producers must fix carbon themselves. Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes and diatoms are photosynthetic single-celled algae; together they form the bulk of ocean phytoplankton and the base of the marine food chain, so 2 and 3 are correct. Copepods are small crustaceans — zooplankton that graze on phytoplankton, hence consumers, not producers. Foraminifera are heterotrophic shelled protists that feed on algae and detritus, so they too sit above the producer level.

answers.value: Hedgehog and pangolin
answers.reasoning: The hedgehog curls into a tight ball so that its spine-covered back faces outward and its soft face and belly are enclosed. The pangolin does exactly the same with its overlapping keratin scales — the behaviour is the origin of its name, from a Malay word meaning 'one that rolls up'. The marmot has no such defence: it is a large burrowing ground squirrel that escapes predators by whistling an alarm call and bolting down its burrow, so statement 2 is wrong and only option D fits.

answers.value: Statements 1, 2 and 4 — endorsed at the 2014 UN Climate Summit, it sets a global timeline to end forest loss and is endorsed by governments, companies and indigenous communities; it is voluntary and India did not sign at inception
answers.reasoning: The New York Declaration on Forests was launched and first endorsed at the UN Climate Summit in New York in September 2014 (statement 1), and it sets out dated goals — halving the loss of natural forests by 2020 and striving to end it by 2030 — which is the global timeline of statement 2. Its endorsers span national and sub-national governments, multinational companies, indigenous peoples' organisations and NGOs, so statement 4 is correct. Statement 3 is false: it is an explicitly voluntary, non-legally-binding political declaration. Statement 5 is also false — India was not among the endorsers at its inception. Since every option other than A carries statement 3 or statement 5, A is the only consistent choice.

answers.value: Brakes of motor vehicles, engines of motor vehicles and power plants only
answers.reasoning: Magnetite nanoparticles of the kind found in brain tissue are combustion- and friction-derived. Brake pads abrading against discs shed iron-oxide particles (1), high-temperature combustion in vehicle engines produces them in exhaust (2), and coal-burning power plants emit them in fly ash (4). Microwave ovens (3) heat food by dielectric absorption and emit no particulate matter at all, and telephone lines (5) are passive conductors carrying no combustion or wear process, so both are excluded — leaving option B.

answers.value: Oyster
answers.reasoning: A filter feeder strains suspended food particles from water. The oyster is a bivalve mollusc that pumps water across its gills and traps plankton and detritus in mucus, the textbook example of filter feeding. Catfish are bottom-foraging omnivores that pick up food items individually, the octopus is an active predator that seizes prey with its arms and beak, and the pelican scoops whole fish in its gular pouch and drains the water off rather than sieving particles.

answers.value: Phosphorus cycle
answers.reasoning: The phosphorus cycle is a purely sedimentary cycle with no significant gaseous phase: the natural reservoir is rock containing phosphates, and weathering releases small quantities of phosphate into the soil solution from which plants absorb it. The carbon and nitrogen cycles both have large atmospheric reservoirs (CO2 and N2 respectively) that supply the cycle, and the sulphur cycle likewise has a substantial atmospheric component from volcanic activity and biogenic gases, so in none of those three is rock weathering the main entry route.

answers.value: Only earthworms, millipedes and woodlice are detritivores (1, 3 and 5 only)
answers.reasoning: Detritivores feed on dead and decaying organic matter. Earthworms (1) ingest soil rich in decomposing litter, millipedes (3) consume decaying leaf litter and plant debris, and woodlice (5) are terrestrial crustaceans that feed on rotting wood and litter — all three qualify. Jellyfish (2) are carnivorous cnidarians that capture live zooplankton and small fish with stinging tentacles, and seahorses (4) are predators that suck in live copepods and small crustaceans; neither feeds on detritus. Hence 1, 3 and 5 only.

answers.value: Assessing the carbon footprint of building operations around the world
answers.reasoning: The Common Carbon Metric was developed under UNEP's Sustainable Buildings and Climate Initiative to provide a consistent international protocol for measuring energy use and reporting greenhouse gas emissions from the operation of buildings, so that building performance can be compared across countries. It is a building-sector measurement protocol, not an agricultural trading instrument (B), a national inventory tool (C), or a global fossil-fuel accounting method (D).

answers.value: All three — cnidarians, fungi and protozoa have species forming symbiotic relationships
answers.reasoning: Cnidarians (1) include reef-building corals and sea anemones, which host symbiotic zooxanthellae and shelter clownfish. Fungi (2) form two of the best-known symbioses in biology: lichens with algae or cyanobacteria, and mycorrhizae with plant roots. Protozoa (3) include the flagellates such as Trichonympha that live in the gut of termites and digest cellulose for their host. All three groups therefore contain symbiotic species.

answers.value: Statements 1 and 4 only are correct
answers.reasoning: The Chausath Yogini temple at Mitaoli near Morena is a circular temple attributed to the Kachchhapaghata ruler Devapala in the early fourteenth century, so 1 is correct, and its circular colonnaded plan is the basis of the widely repeated popular belief that it inspired the design of the Indian Parliament building, so 4 is correct. Statement 2 is false because other circular yogini temples exist in India, notably at Hirapur and Ranipur-Jharial in Odisha and Bhedaghat in Madhya Pradesh. Statement 3 is false because a yogini temple belongs to the Shakta-Tantric tradition and this one houses a Shiva shrine at its centre, not a Vaishnava cult.

answers.value: Dholavira
answers.reasoning: Dholavira, on Khadir island in the Rann of Kutch, is celebrated for the most elaborate water management system of the Harappan world: bunds and dams were thrown across the seasonal Manhar and Mansar streams and the water was channelled into a cascading series of large rock-cut reservoirs built into the settlement itself. Kalibangan is known for its ploughed field and fire altars, Rakhigarhi for its scale and cemetery, and Ropar for being the first Harappan site excavated after Independence.

answers.value: Only Broach had an English East India Company factory in the first quarter of the seventeenth century
answers.reasoning: After the Surat factory of 1613 the English pushed inland and along the Gujarat coast, establishing a factory at Broach (Bharuch) alongside Ahmedabad and Agra within the following few years, so 1 falls inside the first quarter of the century. Trichinopoly (3) is an inland Tamil town that never held an early Company factory; English settlement on the Coromandel began at Masulipatnam and Armagaon and only reached Madras in 1639. Chicacole (2) in northern Andhra is not among the factories founded by 1625, so the answer is 1 only. This is the one item in this set where the negative claim about Chicacole rests on the absence of it from the early factory lists rather than on a positive date, hence the reduced confidence.

answers.value: The later Guptas of Magadha, the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, the Maukharis of Kanauj and the Maitrakas of Valabhi (1, 3, 4 and 6)
answers.reasoning: In the sixth and early seventh centuries northern India was divided among the later Guptas of Magadha (1), the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar (3) whose line produced Harshavardhana himself, the Maukharis of Kanauj (4) whose kingdom Harsha inherited through his sister's marriage, and the Maitrakas of Valabhi (6) in Saurashtra. The Paramaras of Malwa (2) rose only in the ninth to tenth centuries, and the Yadavas of Devagiri (5) belong to the twelfth to fourteenth centuries and to the Deccan, not to northern India, so both are ruled out.

answers.value: All four — wrestling, astrology, accounting and soothsaying
answers.reasoning: Fernao Nuniz's account of the Vijayanagara court describes the large body of women maintained within the palace and lists among them wrestlers, astrologers and soothsayers, and women who wrote all the accounts of the expenses incurred inside the gates as well as the affairs of the kingdom. All four listed accomplishments therefore appear in his description. Confidence is moderate only because the closely similar Portuguese account of Domingo Paes is often quoted alongside Nuniz's and the two are easily conflated.

answers.value: Rabindranath Tagore translated the National Anthem from Bengali to English at Madanapalle
answers.reasoning: While staying at the Besant Theosophical College at Madanapalle in 1919, Tagore rendered Jana Gana Mana into English as 'The Morning Song of India', and the anthem was set to notation there. Pingali Venkayya's flag work is associated with the coastal Andhra region around Machilipatnam and Bezwada, not Madanapalle; Pattabhi Sitaramaiah is likewise linked to coastal Andhra; and the Theosophical Society's headquarters were established at Adyar near Madras, not at Madanapalle.

answers.value: Pairs 2 and 3 only — Chandraketugarh with terracotta art and Ganeshwar with copper artefacts
answers.reasoning: Chandraketugarh in West Bengal is renowned for its richly modelled terracotta plaques and figurines, so pair 2 is correct, and Ganeshwar in the Sikar district of Rajasthan, close to the Khetri copper belt, has yielded a very large assemblage of copper objects, so pair 3 is correct. Burzahom in Kashmir is a Neolithic site known for its pit dwellings, bone and stone tools and a menhir, not for rock-cut shrines, so pair 1 is wrong.

answers.value: Statement 1 only — Chengiz Khan reached the Indus during Iltutmish's reign
answers.reasoning: Chengiz Khan pursued the fugitive Khwarezmian prince Jalaluddin Mangbarni to the Indus in 1221, well within Iltutmish's reign of 1211-1236, so 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong because Timur's invasion, in which he crossed the Indus and sacked Multan and Delhi, took place in 1398 under Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah, roughly half a century after Muhammad bin Tughluq's death. Statement 3 is wrong because Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, decades after Deva Raya II, who ruled Vijayanagara until about 1446.

answers.value: Statements 1 and 3 only are correct
answers.reasoning: St. Francis Xavier was among the small group who joined Ignatius Loyola in founding the Society of Jesus in 1534, so 1 is correct, and his feast on 3 December is observed in Goa every year, with the decennial exposition of his relics, so 3 is correct. Statement 2 is false in its first half: he died in 1552 on Shangchuan (Sancian) island off the coast of China while waiting to enter the mainland, and his body was only later brought to Goa, where it rests in the Basilica of Bom Jesus.

answers.value: Statement 2 only — sons claim during the father's lifetime under Mitakshara but only after his death under Dayabhaga
answers.reasoning: Statement 2 states the central distinction correctly: under Mitakshara a son acquires an interest in ancestral property by birth and can therefore claim during his father's lifetime, whereas under Dayabhaga the son's right arises only on the father's death. Statement 1 is false because the two schools are regional, Dayabhaga prevailing in Bengal and Assam and Mitakshara over the rest of the country, and neither is defined by caste. Statement 3 is false as stated, since the male-only versus mixed-membership contrast is not the basis on which the two schools are distinguished, and the option set contains no combination pairing 2 with 3, which confirms that only 2 is intended to be correct.

answers.value: Playwrights
answers.reasoning: All three were Sanskrit dramatists. Bhavabhuti, of the eighth century, wrote Uttararamacharita, Mahaviracharita and Malatimadhava; Hastimalla was a Jain playwright whose works include Vikranta Kaurava and Maithili Kalyana; and Kshemeshvara wrote the Chandakausika. Their common identity is authorship of plays, not monastic office, temple building or philosophical exposition.

answers.value: Statement 2 only — the Government of India Act, 1935 reserved seats for women in the legislature
answers.reasoning: The Act of 1935 expanded the franchise and provided reserved seats for women in the provincial legislatures, so 2 is correct. Statement 1 is false: the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 did not grant universal adult franchise to women above 21; the vote remained tied to property, tax and educational qualifications, and the question of admitting women at all was left to be decided by the individual provincial legislatures, several of which enfranchised qualified women only in the years that followed.

answers.value: The Quit India Resolution was adopted by the All India Congress Committee on 8 August 1942
answers.reasoning: The AICC met at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay and passed the Quit India Resolution on 8 August 1942; Gandhi delivered the 'Do or Die' call the same evening and the leadership was arrested at dawn on 9 August. The Congress ministries resigned in 1939 over India's entry into the war, and the Cripps Mission with its offer of Dominion Status after the war came in March-April 1942, so options C and D belong to different dates.

answers.value: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
answers.reasoning: 'Songs from Prison' is the collection of English renderings of ancient Indian devotional lyrics that Gandhi made during his imprisonment at Yeravda, published in 1934 in an arrangement prepared by John S. Hoyland. Nehru's prison writings are historical and autobiographical prose rather than translations of religious lyrics, and neither Tilak's Gita Rahasya nor Sarojini Naidu's original English verse fits the description.

answers.value: Paragana - Sarkar - Suba, in ascending order of size
answers.reasoning: In the Mughal administrative hierarchy the empire was divided into subas, each suba into sarkars, and each sarkar into parganas, which were themselves groups of villages. Reading from the smallest upward therefore gives pargana, then sarkar, then suba, which is the order in option A; the other three options invert or scramble this hierarchy.

answers.value: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
answers.reasoning: Vidyasagar served as Secretary of the Hindu Female School founded in Calcutta in 1849 through the efforts of J. E. D. Bethune, and the institution was later renamed the Bethune School after its founder. Annie Besant's educational work belongs to Banaras and a later generation, Debendranath Tagore led the Brahmo Samaj rather than this school, and Sarojini Naidu belongs to the twentieth century entirely.

answers.value: Officers of the Indian National Army
answers.reasoning: Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sehgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon were the three Indian National Army officers court-martialled together at the Red Fort in the winter of 1945-46, the trial that provoked nationwide protest and was defended by a Congress team including Bhulabhai Desai and Tej Bahadur Sapru. They belong to none of the other three contexts listed.

answers.value: Statements 1 and 2 — the Nizamat of Arcot emerged out of Hyderabad State and the Mysore Kingdom out of the Vijayanagara Empire
answers.reasoning: The Carnatic or Arcot Nizamat was carved out of the Deccan territories administered from Hyderabad, its Nawab holding office as a deputy of the Nizam before asserting autonomy, so 1 is correct. The Wodeyars of Mysore were feudatories of Vijayanagara who established an independent kingdom after the empire's collapse following Talikota, so 2 is correct. Statement 3 is false: Rohilkhand was carved out of Mughal Katehar by Rohilla Afghan chiefs under Ali Muhammad Khan in the first half of the eighteenth century, before and independently of Ahmad Shah Durrani's invasions, so it was not formed out of territory he occupied. [Answer corrected to B from the official UPSC answer key; an independent blind derivation had reached A. The reasoning above argues for A and is retained so the disagreement is visible rather than hidden.]

answers.value: Ajanta Caves lie in the gorge of the Waghora river
answers.reasoning: The Ajanta caves are cut into the scarp of a horseshoe-shaped ravine of the Waghora river in the Sahyadri hills, which is exactly what option A states. The Sanchi stupa stands on a hilltop near the Betwa, not in a Chambal gorge; the Pandu-lena caves are near Nashik on the upper Godavari, not the Narmada; and the Amaravati stupa stands on the Krishna, not the Godavari.

answers.value: Statement 2 only — the demand for Bangla as a national language was raised in the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan
answers.reasoning: Statement 2 is correct: Dhirendranath Datta moved in the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan in February 1948 that Bengali be recognised alongside Urdu and English, the demand that grew into the language movement commemorated on 21 February. Statement 1 is false in its attribution: International Mother Language Day was proclaimed by UNESCO, the United Nations body for education, science and culture, and not by UNICEF.

answers.value: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct — permaculture discourages monoculture, avoids the salinity build-up chemical farming causes, and depends on mulching
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: permaculture is built on polyculture and guild planting, while conventional chemical farming is dominated by monoculture. Statement 4 is correct: mulching is a defining permaculture practice (moisture retention, weed suppression, soil-building), and is optional in chemical farming. Statement 3 is wrong the way round — permaculture's mulching, swales and water-harvesting make it well suited to semi-arid regions, whereas chemical farming there depends on heavy irrigation. Statement 2 is the judgement call: chemical fertiliser residues combined with irrigation are a classic cause of secondary salinisation, which permaculture's organic, low-input regime avoids; and once 1 and 4 are accepted, B is the only option containing both.

answers.value: Only statements 2 and 3 are correct — palm oil is used in cosmetics and can yield biodiesel, but the oil palm is native to West Africa, not Southeast Asia
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is false: the oil palm (Elaeis guineensis) is native to West and Central Africa; Indonesia and Malaysia are today's largest producers but are not its native range. Statement 2 is correct — palm oil and its derivatives are standard raw materials in soaps, lipsticks and perfumery. Statement 3 is correct — palm oil is a major biodiesel feedstock. Since statement 1 fails, every option containing it (A, C, D) is eliminated.

answers.value: The Chenab — it receives the Jhelum, Ravi and Sutlej and the combined stream meets the Indus
answers.reasoning: The Jhelum joins the Chenab at Trimmu and the Ravi joins it further downstream; the Sutlej (having already absorbed the Beas) then merges with the Chenab, and the combined river reaches the Indus at Mithankot. So of the four named rivers, three pour into the Chenab. The Jhelum and Ravi are clearly tributaries and cannot be the collector; the Sutlej cannot be either, because neither the Jhelum nor the Ravi flows into it. [Answer corrected to D from the official UPSC answer key; an independent blind derivation had reached A. The reasoning above argues for A and is retained so the disagreement is visible rather than hidden.]

answers.value: Saline lakes — the salt lakes of the Rajasthan (Nagaur/Sambhar) belt
answers.reasoning: Didwana, Kuchaman, Sargol and Khatu are inland salt lakes in the semi-arid Nagaur–Sambhar tract of Rajasthan, worked for common salt. They are inland and far from the coast, which rules out mangrove areas; they lie in a hot desert-margin region, which rules out glaciers; and they are salt-production sites rather than designated wetlands of international importance.

answers.value: The Nagavali and the Vamsadhara rise in the Eastern Ghats
answers.reasoning: The Nagavali and Vamsadhara both rise in the Eastern Ghats of southern Odisha (Kalahandi–Rayagada) and flow south-east into the Bay of Bengal through north Andhra Pradesh. The Brahmani is formed by the union of the Sankh and South Koel and rises in the Chotanagpur plateau, and the Subarnarekha also rises on the Chotanagpur plateau near Ranchi — neither originates in the Eastern Ghats.

answers.value: Only statements 2 and 3 are correct — licences come from the International Seabed Authority, not the Global Ocean Commission
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is false: exploration and mining rights in the international seabed Area are granted by the International Seabed Authority, a UNCLOS body; the Global Ocean Commission was a short-lived independent advocacy initiative with no licensing power. Statement 2 is correct — India holds ISA contracts for polymetallic nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin and for polymetallic sulphides on the Indian Ocean ridges. Statement 3 is correct — rare earth elements occur in deep-sea muds and in the crusts and nodules of the international seabed.

answers.value: Sugarcane — it consumes far more water per unit of produce than the alternatives
answers.reasoning: Sugarcane is a long-duration, high-biomass crop needing roughly 1,500–2,500 mm of water per season, and is the standard example of a water-guzzling crop in Indian irrigation policy. Pearl millet and red gram are drought-hardy dryland crops grown largely on residual moisture, and sunflower has a moderate, much shorter water demand. 'Least water-efficient' means most water per unit output, which is sugarcane.

answers.value: Both statements are correct — trade winds warm the western tropical oceans, westerlies warm the eastern temperate oceans
answers.reasoning: In the tropics the trade winds blow from east to west and drag warm surface water westward, piling up warm pools on the western side (for example the western Pacific warm pool) while cold upwelling keeps the eastern margins cool off Peru and Namibia — so statement 1 holds. In the temperate belt the prevailing westerlies drive warm water eastward, which is why the North Atlantic Drift makes the eastern Atlantic and north-west Europe far milder than the western side at the same latitude — so statement 2 holds.

answers.value: All three statements are correct — the Climate-Smart Village approach is a CCAFS project, CCAFS runs under CGIAR (headquartered in Montpellier, France), and ICRISAT is a CGIAR centre
answers.reasoning: The Climate-Smart Village model was developed and piloted in India under the CGIAR research programme on Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security, so statement 1 is correct. CCAFS is one of the CGIAR research programmes and the CGIAR System Organization is headquartered at Montpellier, France, so statement 2 is correct. ICRISAT, with its headquarters at Patancheru near Hyderabad, is one of the CGIAR research centres, so statement 3 is correct.

answers.value: Tropical rain forest
answers.reasoning: Rapid litter decomposition leaving a nearly bare soil surface, plus a flora dominated by lianas that climb to the canopy and by epiphytes rooted on upper branches, are diagnostic of the warm, humid, closed-canopy tropical rain forest. Coniferous forests accumulate thick slow-rotting needle litter; dry deciduous forests have a marked leafless season and little epiphytic growth; mangroves are halophytic, waterlogged and dominated by stilt-rooted trees rather than climbers and epiphytes.

answers.value: Fire, grazing herbivores and seasonal rainfall keep tree cover in check in savannahs
answers.reasoning: Recurrent dry-season fire kills tree seedlings while grasses resprout from underground buds; browsing and grazing herbivores suppress woody regeneration; and a strongly seasonal rainfall regime with a long dry period gives deep-rooted grasses the advantage over trees. These three are the standard maintenance mechanisms of the savannah biome. Soil properties and termite activity do influence savannah structure locally, which makes this item genuinely arguable — but they are secondary to the fire–herbivory–seasonality triad, and no option offers all five factors.

answers.value: Only statement 2 is correct — polar ice and glaciers exceed groundwater, but rivers and lakes hold far less than groundwater
answers.reasoning: Of the Earth's fresh water, ice caps and glaciers hold roughly two-thirds and groundwater roughly one-third, so statement 2 is correct. Rivers and lakes together account for well under one percent of fresh water — orders of magnitude less than groundwater — so statement 1 is false.

answers.value: Statements 3, 4 and 5 are correct; moringa is not a legume and tamarind is not endemic to South Asia
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is false: moringa belongs to the family Moringaceae, not to the legume family. Statement 2 is false: tamarind is native to tropical Africa and was introduced into South Asia long ago, so it is naturalised rather than endemic. Statement 3 is correct — tamarind is gathered largely from forests and is notified as a minor forest produce. Statement 4 is correct — India exports both tamarind and moringa seed. Statement 5 is correct — moringa seed oil is a well-studied biodiesel feedstock and tamarind kernel oil has also been trialled for the purpose.

answers.value: Fissure volcanic rock — the Deccan Trap basalts
answers.reasoning: Black cotton soil, or regur, is the residual soil of the Deccan Trap country of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, produced by the in-situ weathering of basaltic lava erupted through fissure eruptions. Its clay content and high iron and magnesium reflect that basaltic parent material. Granite and schist weather to red and lateritic soils, shale and limestone to different residual soils, and brown forest soil is a soil type rather than a parent rock.

answers.value: Both statements are correct — recombinant vector vaccines are made by genetic engineering and use both bacterial and viral vectors
answers.reasoning: A recombinant vector vaccine is made by inserting the gene for a pathogen's antigen into a harmless carrier organism, which is by definition genetic engineering, so statement 1 is correct. Both viral vectors, such as adenovirus and vesicular stomatitis virus, and bacterial vectors, such as attenuated Salmonella and BCG, are in use as carriers, so statement 2 is correct.

answers.value: Both statements are correct — mitochondrial replacement can be done before or after fertilisation, and mitochondria are inherited from the mother
answers.reasoning: Mitochondrial replacement therapy has two forms: maternal spindle transfer, done on the unfertilised egg before in-vitro fertilisation, and pronuclear transfer, done on the zygote after fertilisation — so statement 1 is correct. Mitochondria in the embryo come from the egg cytoplasm, and the few paternal mitochondria that enter with the sperm are destroyed, so mitochondrial DNA and the disorders it carries pass down the maternal line only, making statement 2 correct.

answers.value: Developing genetically modified crop plants — the Bt cotton events
answers.reasoning: Bollgard I and Bollgard II are transgenic cotton technologies carrying insecticidal genes from Bacillus thuringiensis — Cry1Ac in the first and Cry1Ac plus Cry2Ab in the second — for resistance to bollworms. They are genetic-modification events in a crop plant, not a tissue-culture propagation method, a growth-regulator product, or a biofertiliser.

answers.value: Only the area of the vent hole and the weight of the lid/regulator matter; flame temperature does not
answers.reasoning: Steam escapes only when its pressure lifts the weight on the vent, so the operating pressure is fixed by that weight divided by the area of the hole; the boiling point, and hence the cooking temperature, follows from that pressure. A hotter flame merely raises steam faster and makes the vent release more often — it cannot push the temperature past the pressure-set boiling point — so statement 2 is wrong, leaving statements 1 and 3.

answers.value: Only bacteria and fungi can be grown in artificial media; viruses cannot
answers.reasoning: Bacteria and fungi are free-living organisms with their own metabolic machinery and grow readily on nutrient agar, Sabouraud medium and similar synthetic media. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with no ribosomes or metabolism of their own and can multiply only inside a living host cell, so they are cultivated in cell cultures, embryonated eggs or animals — never in a cell-free artificial medium.

answers.value: Only statement 2 is correct — adenovirus causes some common colds and HIV is a retrovirus, but the genome descriptions in statement 1 are wrong
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong twice over: adenoviruses have a double-stranded DNA genome, not single-stranded, and retroviruses carry a single-stranded RNA genome which they reverse-transcribe into DNA after entering the host cell. Statement 2 is correct: adenoviruses are among the agents that cause common colds and respiratory infections, and AIDS is caused by HIV, a retrovirus.

answers.value: Because the water molecule is dipolar (polar) in nature
answers.reasoning: The bent geometry of the water molecule and the electronegativity difference between oxygen and hydrogen give it a permanent dipole, so its partially negative oxygen surrounds cations and its partially positive hydrogens surround anions, pulling ionic and polar solutes into solution. This is why water is called the universal solvent. Thermal conductivity and specific heat capacity describe how water handles heat, not how it solvates solutes, and simply being an oxide of hydrogen says nothing about solvent power.

answers.value: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; sodium lamps do not outlast LEDs
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: a sodium lamp radiates in all directions and needs reflectors to aim the light downward, whereas an LED is inherently directional. Statement 3 is correct: low-pressure sodium light is essentially monochromatic yellow with very poor colour rendering, while LEDs can be tuned across the spectrum and give far better colour rendering on streets. Statement 2 is the wrong way round — LED street lights are rated for roughly 50,000 hours or more against about 20,000–24,000 for high-pressure sodium, which is a main reason for the switch to LEDs.

answers.value: Spread of viral diseases — ACE2 is the cell-surface receptor the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binds
answers.reasoning: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 is a membrane protein of lung, gut and vascular cells that normally regulates blood pressure through the renin–angiotensin system, and it is the receptor by which SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 enter human cells. Its distribution therefore explains the tissue tropism and spread of COVID-19. It has nothing to do with transgenes in crops, with satellite navigation, or with wildlife telemetry.

answers.value: Polycarbonate
answers.reasoning: Bisphenol A is a monomer polymerised with phosgene to make polycarbonate, and it is also a building block of epoxy resins used to line food and beverage cans. Its leaching from polycarbonate bottles and can linings is the source of the health concern. Low-density polyethylene and polyvinyl chloride are made from ethylene and vinyl chloride respectively, and polyethylene terephthalate is made from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol — none uses bisphenol A.

answers.value: Toiletries — antibacterial soaps, toothpaste, hand washes and similar personal-care products
answers.reasoning: Triclosan is a synthetic antibacterial and antifungal agent added to personal-care products such as antibacterial soaps, hand washes, toothpaste, deodorants and cosmetics, and concern over it centres on endocrine disruption and antimicrobial resistance from long exposure. It is not a permitted food preservative, has no role in fruit ripening (which involves ethylene-releasing agents), and is not a leachate associated with reused plastic containers, where the concern is bisphenol A and phthalates.

answers.value: Because the speed of light is a constant, a light-year is a fixed, well-defined distance
answers.reasoning: A light-year is defined as the distance light travels in one year, so it is a usable unit of length only because the speed of light in vacuum is an invariant constant (about 3 x 10^8 m/s). If c varied, the same 'light-year' would stand for different distances at different times and places, and the unit would be meaningless. A is false and irrelevant (stellar distances do change). B is irrelevant to a unit of length. C is both false in general (light is bent by gravity) and beside the point, since the definition depends on the light's speed, not the shape of its path.

answers.value: Both are true: Indian Parliament's legislative power is limited, and constitutionality of an amendment goes to a Constitution Bench
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the British Parliament is sovereign and no court may invalidate its Acts, whereas Indian Parliament legislates within a written Constitution and is limited by the federal distribution of powers, Part III, and judicial review. Statement 2 reflects Article 145(3), which requires a bench of at least five judges (a Constitution Bench) to decide any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, which is the route every challenge to an amendment Act has taken from Kesavananda Bharati onwards. The judgement call is that Article 145(3) is conditional rather than automatic, so statement 2 is worded more absolutely than the Article, but as a description of how India differs from Britain it stands.

answers.value: Both statements about the Union Government's administrative-reform machinery are correct
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar's 1950 Report on the Reorganisation of the Machinery of Government recommended that a Minister and a Secretary be earmarked exclusively for pursuing and promoting administrative reform. Statement 2 is correct: acting on the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966), the Department of Personnel was created in August 1970 within the Cabinet Secretariat and therefore under the Prime Minister's charge; it later became the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, still held by the Prime Minister. The residual doubt is only over the precise wording attributed to the 1950 report, which is why this is not marked HIGH. answers.value: Article 21
answers.reasoning: In K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) a nine-judge Bench held unanimously that the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected intrinsically as part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and as part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III. Article 15 deals with non-discrimination, Article 19 with the six freedoms, and Article 29 with protection of the interests of minorities, none of which is the anchoring provision the Court identified.

answers.value: Statements 2 and 3 — reclaiming public space and participation, and non-denial of services to unauthorised colonies
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: 'Right to the City' is a concept advanced by Lefebvre and taken up by urban movements and the New Urban Agenda; it is not a codified, agreed human right and UN-Habitat runs no country-by-country monitoring of commitments under it. Statement 2 is the core of the idea — the right of every inhabitant to appropriate and reclaim urban public space and to participate in decisions about the city. Statement 3 follows from the inclusive reading of the concept, under which all inhabitants including those in informal or unauthorised settlements are entitled to basic public services regardless of tenure status. Note that on a strict reading only statement 2 is unambiguously right, but 'the 2 only' combination is not offered, and of the two remaining candidates statement 3 is far more defensible than statement 1.

answers.value: Only statement 2 — police need court approval to interrogate an accused in judicial custody
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong on the crucial detail: in judicial custody the accused is committed to the magistrate's custody and lodged in JAIL (judicial lock-up), not in a police station; it is police custody in which the accused is kept at the police station. Statement 2 is correct: once an accused is in judicial custody the investigating officer cannot interrogate him at will and must obtain the court's permission to do so.

answers.value: Only statement 2 — parole is not a right, but State Governments do have their own parole rules
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: parole is a discretionary concession and not an enforceable right, and the Model Prison Manual expressly says it may be refused even where the prisoner makes out a sufficient case if the competent authority is satisfied that his release would not be in the interest of society. Statement 2 is correct: prisons are a State subject (Entry 4, State List), so each State frames its own Prisoners Release on Parole rules, such as the Delhi Prison Rules or the Punjab Good Conduct Prisoners' Probational Release Act.

answers.value: Ministry of Tribal Affairs
answers.reasoning: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 is administered by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, which is the nodal agency at the national level for its implementation and for issuing guidelines to States. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change administers forest and wildlife law and is a frequent distractor here, but it does not administer the Forest Rights Act; the Ministry of Panchayati Raj administers PESA, and Rural Development has no role.

answers.value: Article 14
answers.reasoning: A law that hands the executive unguided and uncontrolled discretion permits arbitrary and unequal application, and arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality — the doctrine settled in E. P. Royappa and Maneka Gandhi, under which Article 14 strikes down conferral of naked, unchannelled discretionary power. Article 28 concerns religious instruction in State-funded institutions, Article 32 is the remedy for enforcing rights rather than a substantive guarantee, and Article 44 is a non-justiciable Directive Principle on a uniform civil code.

answers.value: The Union Legislature contains elected representatives of the constituent units (Rajya Sabha)
answers.reasoning: The defining federal feature is that the constituent units are represented as units in the federal legislature — in India the Rajya Sabha, whose members are elected by the elected members of the State legislative assemblies, mirroring the US Senate and the German Bundesrat. An independent judiciary (option A) supports federalism by providing an umpire for Centre-State disputes, but it exists equally in unitary states such as the United Kingdom and so does not by itself indicate a federal character. Option C describes a political convention, not a constitutional feature, and option D concerns rights enforcement, which is unrelated to the federal-unitary axis. [Answer corrected to A from the official UPSC answer key; an independent blind derivation had reached B. The reasoning above argues for B and is retained so the disagreement is visible rather than hidden.]

answers.value: A community of persons, a definite territory, independence of external control, and an organised government
answers.reasoning: The standard definition of a State requires exactly four elements — population, definite territory, government, and sovereignty — and option A is the only one that names all four, with 'independent of external control' supplying sovereignty. Option B omits sovereignty and drifts into the purposes of the State rather than its definition. Option C describes a nation (shared culture and tradition) rather than a State and again omits sovereignty. Option D describes the internal architecture of a particular kind of government and likewise leaves out independence from external control.

answers.value: Both — a retired SC judge can be recalled under Article 128, and a High Court can review its own judgement
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 tracks Article 128: the Chief Justice of India may, with the previous consent of the President, request a person who has held office as a Judge of the Supreme Court to sit and act as a Judge of the Supreme Court. Statement 2 is correct in substance: while Article 137 expressly confers review power on the Supreme Court, a High Court is a court of record under Article 215 and has been held to possess the power to review its own judgements, reinforced by Section 114 and Order XLVII of the Civil Procedure Code. The judgement calls are that Article 128 also needs the retired judge's own consent, which statement 1 omits, and that a High Court's review power in criminal matters is constrained by Section 362 CrPC — hence MED rather than HIGH. [Answer corrected to A from the official UPSC answer key; an independent blind derivation had reached C. The reasoning above argues for C and is retained so the disagreement is visible rather than hidden.]

answers.value: Only statement 1 — India has single citizenship and a single domicile
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: unlike the United States, India confers only one citizenship, that of the Union, and the Supreme Court has held there is only one domicile, the domicile of India, with no separate State domicile. Statement 2 is wrong: Article 58 requires the President merely to be a citizen of India, not a citizen by birth, so a naturalised or registered citizen is eligible — the 'natural-born' requirement belongs to the US Constitution. Statement 3 is wrong: Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 allows deprivation of citizenship acquired by registration or naturalisation on grounds such as fraud, disloyalty, trading with the enemy, or imprisonment within five years.

answers.value: Separation of powers
answers.reasoning: The classical safeguard of liberty, following Montesquieu, is the separation of powers with its accompanying checks and balances, which prevents any single organ from accumulating the power to act arbitrarily. A 'committed judiciary' is the opposite of a safeguard, since a judiciary committed to the ruling ideology cannot restrain it. Centralisation of powers is precisely the condition liberty is safeguarded against, and an elected government, while necessary, can itself be majoritarian and oppressive without institutional restraints.

answers.value: the Directive Principles of State Policy
answers.reasoning: Article 39(c), a Directive Principle, requires the State to direct its policy towards ensuring that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment; Article 39(b) is its companion on distribution of material resources. Concentration of wealth therefore offends the Directive Principles rather than the Right to Equality or the Right to Freedom, neither of which addresses economic distribution.

answers.value: A legal (constitutional) right available to any person, not only citizens
answers.reasoning: The 44th Constitutional Amendment, 1978 deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, removing property from the list of Fundamental Rights, and inserted Article 300A in Part XII: 'No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.' The wording is 'no person', not 'no citizen', so the right is available to non-citizens as well, which rules out options A and C; and since it is expressly retained in the Constitution as a legal right, option D is also wrong.

answers.value: A Sovereign Democratic Republic
answers.reasoning: As adopted, the Preamble described India as a 'SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC'. The words 'SOCIALIST' and 'SECULAR' were inserted only by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, so they formed no part of India's constitutional status on 26 January 1950. Option A drops sovereignty, which was present from the start, and options C and D read the 1976 additions back into 1950.

answers.value: A government limited by the terms of the Constitution
answers.reasoning: Constitutional government, or constitutionalism, means limited government: the rulers derive their authority from the Constitution and are bound by the restraints it imposes, so power is exercised within legal limits rather than arbitrarily. It is not defined by federalism (option A), nor by whether the Head of State is nominal (option B) or wields real power (option C) — a constitutional government can be unitary or federal, parliamentary or presidential; what makes it constitutional is the limitation.

answers.value: tribal languages
answers.reasoning: All three are tribal languages of central and eastern India: Halbi is an Indo-Aryan language of the Bastar region of Chhattisgarh, Ho is an Austroasiatic (Munda) language spoken chiefly in Jharkhand and Odisha, and Kui is a Dravidian language of the Kondh people of Odisha. That they belong to three different language families, yet are all spoken by tribal communities, is exactly the pattern the question is testing.

answers.value: All three statements are not correct
answers.reasoning: Note the question asks which statements are NOT correct. Statement 1 is not correct: in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996) the Supreme Court held that Bharat Ratna and the Padma Awards are not 'titles' within the meaning of Article 18(1) and so are constitutionally valid, though they may not be used as prefixes or suffixes to a recipient's name. Statement 2 is not correct: the Padma Awards, instituted in 1954, were suspended twice — from 1977 to 1980, and again from 1992 to 1995 pending litigation — not once. Statement 3 is not correct: the ceiling on Bharat Ratna awards is three in a particular year, not five.

answers.value: Statement 1 is wrong on the recognising agency (FAO, not UNCDF); Statement 2 is correct
answers.reasoning: Hyderabad was indeed named a 2020 Tree City of the World, but the programme is run jointly by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the Arbor Day Foundation — not by the UN Capital Development Fund, which finances development in least-developed countries and has nothing to do with urban forestry. Statement 1 therefore fails on the agency it names. Statement 2 is correct: Tree Cities of the World recognition is conferred for one year at a time against five core standards of commitment to growing and maintaining urban forests, and must be renewed annually.

answers.value: Statements 1 and 3 — Tiger Woods was the first winner and Roger Federer has won it most often
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: at the inaugural Laureus World Sports Awards in 2000, the World Sportsman of the Year went to the American golfer Tiger Woods. Statement 3 is correct: Roger Federer has won the World Sportsman of the Year more times than anyone else, taking it in 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008 and 2018. Statement 2 is wrong: tennis players dominate the roll of honour — Federer, Djokovic and Nadal between them account for the largest share — whereas Formula One drivers (Schumacher, Vettel, Hamilton) have won it far fewer times.

answers.value: Only statement 2 — the five new sports were included; the motto was not 'A New World'
answers.reasoning: The 32nd Summer Olympics were the Games of the XXXII Olympiad, Tokyo 2020, held in 2021. Statement 1 is wrong: the official motto adopted for these Games was 'United by Emotion'. Statement 2 is correct: Tokyo 2020 added five sports to the programme — baseball/softball, karate, skateboarding, sport climbing and surfing — of which skateboarding, sport climbing and surfing made their Olympic debut.

answers.value: Neither — finalists were decided by percentage of points won, and England actually won more matches than New Zealand
answers.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: after COVID-19 disrupted the 2019-21 cycle and left teams having played very unequal numbers of series, the ICC ranked sides by the PERCENTAGE of available points won, not by the raw number of matches won, and it was on that percentage that India and New Zealand reached the final. Statement 2 is wrong twice over: New Zealand finished ahead of England on points percentage, and in absolute terms England won more Test matches in the cycle than New Zealand did, since England played roughly twice as many matches.
